title: Reshape Data: Melt
statement:
LeetCode poses this one in pandas, on a DataFrame named `report`; here the DataFrame is a table and you answer with one MySQL query.

- `report(product, quarter_1, quarter_2, quarter_3, quarter_4)`: one row per product in **wide** form. `product` is the product's name and is never null; each `quarter_k` column holds that product's sales in quarter k. A sales figure may be null when it is missing.

Turn the table into **long** form: every row of `report` becomes four rows, one per quarter, with the columns `product`, `quarter` and `sales`. `quarter` is the name of the source column as text (`'quarter_1'`, `'quarter_2'`, `'quarter_3'` or `'quarter_4'`) and `sales` is the value that column held, kept even when it is null. The result therefore has exactly four times as many rows as `report`. Rows may come in any order.
constraints: Sales figures are integers and may be null
Each input row yields exactly four output rows, one per quarter column
reference:
SELECT product, 'quarter_1' AS quarter, quarter_1 AS sales
FROM report
UNION ALL
SELECT product, 'quarter_2', quarter_2
FROM report
UNION ALL
SELECT product, 'quarter_3', quarter_3
FROM report
UNION ALL
SELECT product, 'quarter_4', quarter_4
FROM report;
brute:
WITH quarters (quarter) AS (
  SELECT 'quarter_1' UNION ALL SELECT 'quarter_2' UNION ALL SELECT 'quarter_3' UNION ALL SELECT 'quarter_4'
)
SELECT
  r.product,
  q.quarter,
  CASE q.quarter
    WHEN 'quarter_1' THEN r.quarter_1
    WHEN 'quarter_2' THEN r.quarter_2
    WHEN 'quarter_3' THEN r.quarter_3
    ELSE r.quarter_4
  END AS sales
FROM report AS r
CROSS JOIN quarters AS q
notes:
## Intuition

In pandas this is `report.melt(id_vars=['product'], var_name='quarter', value_name='sales')`: the identifier column stays, and every other column is turned into a (column name, value) pair on its own row. SQL has no melt, but the four quarter columns are fixed and known, so each one can be read by its own `SELECT` that pairs the product with a constant naming the column. `UNION ALL` stacks the four blocks.

## Approach

1. The first `SELECT` takes every product with the literal `'quarter_1'` as `quarter` and the `quarter_1` value as `sales`; its aliases name the result's columns.
2. `UNION ALL` appends the same shape for `quarter_2`, then `quarter_3`, then `quarter_4`. Later blocks need no aliases, because a union takes its column names from the first query.

## Example 1, step by step

- Block 1: (Umbrella, quarter_1, 417), (SleepingBag, quarter_1, 800).
- Block 2: (Umbrella, quarter_2, 224), (SleepingBag, quarter_2, 936).
- Block 3: (Umbrella, quarter_3, 379), (SleepingBag, quarter_3, 93).
- Block 4: (Umbrella, quarter_4, 611), (SleepingBag, quarter_4, 875).

Stacked, these are the eight expected rows.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n) for n rows in `report`; the table is scanned four times.
- Space: O(n) for the 4n output rows.

## Pitfalls

- Plain `UNION` removes duplicates: two report rows for the same product with the same figure in some quarter would collapse into one output row.
- Do not filter out null sales; melt keeps a row for a missing figure.
- The `quarter` value is the column's name as a string literal (`'quarter_1'`), not the column itself; writing `quarter_1 AS quarter` would put the number there.

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `'quarter_k'` | constant text naming the column a block reads |
| `quarter` | output column holding that constant |
| `sales` | output column holding the product's figure for that quarter |
| `UNION ALL` | stacks the four blocks and keeps every row |

narration.1: The first block pairs each product with the constant quarter_1 and its quarter_1 figure; these aliases name the output columns.
narration.2: Every row of report contributes to every block.
narration.3: UNION ALL appends the next block without removing duplicate rows.
narration.4: The second block reads quarter_2 the same way; its column names come from the first block.
narration.10: The last block reads quarter_4, completing four rows per product.
